tip: θα περάσω από την τράπεζα (tha peráso apó tin trápeza) – lit. 'I'll pass from the bank': περνάω από (pernáo apó) is how you say stop by.
θα κοιμηθώ (tha kimithó = I'll sleep) – the ending looks passive, but this verb has no other shape: sleeping just comes in passive form.
δεν θα βγω (den tha vgo = I won't go out) – 'not' goes first, before the future word, never between it and the verb.
θα σου πω (tha su po = I'll tell you) – the little word for 'you' slips in between the future marker and the verb.
θα σε περιμένω (tha se periméno = I'll wait for you) – Greek drops the 'for': you wait someone, directly.
θα σου αρέσει (tha su arési = it will please you) – liking works backwards: the island does the pleasing, you're on the receiving end.
'On foot' is lit. 'with the feet': θα πάμε με τα πόδια (tha páme me ta pódia = we'll go with the feet).
Countries wear the article: στην Ελλάδα (stin Elláda) – lit. 'to the Greece'. Greek puts 'the' before country names.
θα βρέξει (tha vréksi = it will rain) – no 'it' anywhere: the verb alone is the full sentence for weather.
θα αργήσει (tha argísi = it will be late) – being late is a verb in Greek, so 'be' disappears into one word.
No 'a' before professions: θα γίνει καλή γιατρός (tha gíni kalí giatrós) – lit. 'she'll become good doctor', no article needed.
Θα δούμε τι θα γίνει (tha dúme ti tha gíni = we'll see what will happen) – Greek keeps the future in both halves where English switches to 'happens'.
θα ζητήσω αύξηση από το αφεντικό (tha zitíso áfksisi apó to afentikó) – you ask something FROM someone in Greek, not ask someone for it.
θα μάθουμε κολύμπι στα εγγόνια (tha máthume kolýmbi sta engónia) – μαθαίνω (mathéno) means both learn and teach; 'to the grandkids' flips it to teaching.
